items.transcript: I lost 20 pounds during both of my pregnancies because I was so nauseous and had such intense food aversions. So before we even start trying for baby number three, there are a few things I'm going to be doing differently. This time around, I'm trying to go into pregnancy feeling as strong, nourished, and replenished as I possibly can. One thing I've already done differently was just give my body more time. My son is 28 months now, and he's been done breastfeeding for about four months. So this is my first time in like five years that I've actually had a break where I haven't been pregnant or breastfeeding. So my hormones have finally had a chance to settle, and my body's had a bit of a time to actually recover. I've also been really intentional about eating nutrient-dense foods that actually fuel my body. And for me, this also means paying attention to which foods don't feel good in my body. Every single time I eat gluten or sugar, I notice that I'm achier, that I'm irritable, overall feel like inflamed and gross, which I don't want to be feeling like. I'm also trying to replenish any nutrients that I'm low in instead of guessing. So I do blood work twice a year through Function Health, which has helped me identify some areas I personally need to work on. For example, my omega levels were really low. So I've been supplementing with omegas as well as adding more salmon into my diet, and those levels have been going up. There are a few other things that I also supplement based on my labs, but what I really like is having actual information about what my body needs instead of just like randomly taking things. I've also started taking an egg quality supplement, and my husband has started taking a sperm support supplement just to get things as optimal as possible. And probably the biggest thing for me has been consistently exercising. My goal is not to be ripped, not to be tiny, I just want to go into pregnancy feeling strong. The stronger I am, the more muscle I have supporting my body, the better equipped I feel for all of the changes that pregnancy brings. Obviously, I have no idea if any of this is going to make pregnancy number three easier. If you've had a really hard pregnancy before, I'd love to know, was there anything that you did differently before your next one that you felt like really made a difference?

Recipe 👇🏼 

Ingredients: 
-12 Sourdough English Muffins 
-12 Eggs 
-1/4 Milk
-12 slices Cheddar Cheese 
-8oz Cottage Cheese
-Nitrate free Bacon 
*add any meats, cheeses, or veggies that you like! 

Directions: 
-Preheat oven to 325 degrees F. Spray a 9x13-inch pan with cooking spray.
-Beat the eggs, milk, cottage cheese, cooked bacon/meats, salt, and pepper together in a large bowl using a fork, whisk, or hand mixer. 
-Pour into the prepared pan and bake for 18-22 minutes, (or forget about it like me and take it out in a panic). Cool before cutting into 12 circles or squares. 
-Top 12 of the english muffin halves with the eggs and cheese then top with the other muffin halves to make 12 sandwiches.
-Individually wrap each sandwich with waxed paper, aluminum foil, or parchment paper and freeze, sealed in a large ziploc bag, for up to 1 month.

items.caption:
I didn’t realize how many decisions came with labor… until I actually looked into it.

Here are some things you may be asked about during labor (especially in a hospital setting) that are worth understanding ahead of time:

Labor Positioning
Providers may suggest different positions to make it easier to assist — but you can choose what feels most comfortable and natural. (Yes, you can say no to lying on your back.)

Episiotomy
Used to speed up delivery, but research shows natural tearing often heals better and is less severe.

Eating & Drinking
Some providers or hospital policies may not allow it, but labor is physically demanding — staying fueled and hydrated can help maintain energy.

Cervical Checks
Measure dilation and labor progress.
Some women choose to limit or decline since progress isn’t always linear — you can be dilated for days or weeks before active labor begins.

Pitocin
Used to induce or strengthen contractions.
It can help move labor along, but may also lead to more interventions. Some women choose to decline to let their body regulate contractions naturally.

Breaking Your Water
Sometimes used to speed up labor if it has stalled.
Others decline due to increased risk of infection and more intense contractions.

IV’s
Used for hydration and quick access if medication is needed.
Some women decline so they can move freely (which can make a BIG difference in labor).

Monitoring
Continuous monitoring is standard in many hospitals, especially with medicated births.
Some choose intermittent monitoring for more freedom of movement and fewer unnecessary interventions.

Epidurals
A very common form of pain management.
Some women decline to stay mobile, avoid risks, or have an unmedicated experience.

Induction
More common than ever. While sometimes medically necessary, some women choose to wait for spontaneous labor to avoid a cascade of interventions.
(You can always say no.)

And if you’re unsure in the moment, you can always ask:

→ Is this necessary right now?
→ What are my alternatives?
→ What happens if we wait?

items.transcript: Nobody warned me that deciding whether to have a third baby would be way harder than deciding to have the first two. Because with the first two, I knew exactly why I wanted them. Deciding to have our first was a no-brainer. I knew I wanted to be mom. I knew I wanted kids. Deciding to have our second felt pretty straightforward, too. We knew we wanted more than one. We wanted our daughter to have a sibling. We already pictured our family with multiple kids. But the third? This feels completely different. Because honestly, nothing is missing right now. We have two incredible kids. They've got each other. We're past the newborn stage. We have routines. We can travel. Our house works. Financially, things work for us. Life feels really good. And adding a third baby doesn't necessarily make any of those things better on paper. We'd be outnumbered. Our space would be stretched. Our finances would be stretched. Plus going through pregnancy again and diapers and the newborn stage and all of those things. And I think that's where I keep getting stuck. But I heard someone once say to picture your dinner table 10 years from now. And how many people are there? And I keep going back to that. Because life feels really good right now. But I don't want to look back in a few years and feel like somebody's missing from our table. I just genuinely don't know.

items.caption:
I found this video from almost 5 years ago 🤯 but I still remember this moment like it happened yesterday. 

We waited my entire pregnancy to find out if our first baby was a boy or a girl.

And in my head, I had definitely built up this movie-worthy moment where the baby would be born, someone would yell “IT’S A ___!” and we’d both burst into tears. 😂

Except… that’s not what happened at all.

She was born, they put her on my chest, and for probably the first 15 minutes we genuinely had NO idea whether we had a son or a daughter. And we didn’t care. 😂

We were looking at her face, talking to her, soaking in the fact that there was suddenly an actual HUMAN lying on my chest after all those months of wondering who was in there.

Eventually one of the nurses was basically like… “Wait, is it a girl or boy?” Oh. Right. 😂 I looked and it was A GIRL! 

But I remember being surprised by how uneventful that part felt. 👆

Not because we weren’t excited to have a daughter — we obviously were — but because in that moment, “boy or girl” suddenly felt so much smaller than I had imagined it would.

Did you find out during pregnancy or wait until birth? And if you waited… was the reveal as dramatic as you imagined it would be? 😂

#pregnancy #pregnant #birth #naturalbirth #relatablemom

My husband is scared that having a third baby could be a mistake.And the weirdest part is… I understand that fear more than he probably realizes.

When I was pregnant with our second, I remember genuinely wondering if we had made a mistake too.

I loved our daughter SO much that I could not wrap my head around how another baby could possibly fit into our family without changing everything I loved about it.

I worried I wouldn’t love him the same. I worried he would never “live up” to the relationship I already had with her. And even at 8 months pregnant, I was still having those thoughts.

Then he was born. And of course, now I look at him and cannot imagine our family without him.

But I also don’t think that means every fear about having another baby should automatically be dismissed with “you’ll never regret the baby once they’re here.”

Because deciding whether to have a third feels different.

We already love our life. We love our family dynamic. We know how much another baby would change our time, energy, finances, routines, travel… basically everything.

So lately my husband and I have been having some really deep conversations about what we actually want our family to look like.

I’m curious though — if you have 3+ kids, did you feel completely sure before trying for another… or did you have a lot of fear too?

items.caption:
9 cm dilated with my first baby and completely unmedicated. And somehow… I still felt incredibly calm and confident in what my body was doing. 🤍

I share my births because I think women deserve to see more examples of birth that aren’t centered around fear.

That doesn’t mean I believe everyone needs to have an unmedicated birth.

I believe women deserve to understand their options, know what questions to ask, make a birth plan, build a support system they trust, and walk into birth feeling like an active participant in their care — not like birth is just something that happens to them.

Before my first birth, I spent so much time learning about labor, interventions, pain management, positioning, advocacy, and what I wanted my birth environment to feel like.

Did everything go exactly according to plan? Of course not. But having a plan wasn’t about controlling every detail.

It was about knowing my preferences, understanding my options, and feeling confident enough to make decisions when things changed. And honestly, that philosophy has carried into so much of motherhood for me. I don’t want someone else to tell me what I’m supposed to do.

I want good information.
I want to understand my options.
I want to ask questions.
And then I want to feel confident making the decision that works best for my family.

If that sounds like you too, come hang out on my page. 🤍

I share a lot more birth footage like this, pregnancy + postpartum, motherhood, and everything I’m learning along the way as I try to make informed decisions for my family without feeling like I have to do motherhood exactly like everyone else.

And if you’re pregnant right now, I have a free unmedicated birth guide plus more resources linked in my bio to help you feel more prepared going into birth.

items.caption:
One of the coolest things about labor is realizing just how much your body is doing behind the scenes. 🤯

During unmedicated labor, your body releases hormones like oxytocin and endorphins that help you cope with contractions — and for some women, that can create this incredibly relaxed, floaty, almost euphoric feeling between them.

This was me 😂 Completely in my own little world.

And I think this is something we don’t talk about enough.

Birth is so often portrayed as something terrifying that happens to you, when in reality, your body has some pretty incredible systems designed to help you through it.

That doesn’t mean birth is painless. It doesn’t mean every labor looks like this. And there is absolutely no “right” way to give birth.

But I wish more women went into birth knowing what their bodies are capable of instead of only hearing everything that could go wrong.

Follow along for more positive, empowering birth education + real-life motherhood 🤍

#positivebirth #unmedicatedbirth #birthstory #naturalbirth #naturalbirthing

items.caption:
yes, labor can last hours—but you’re not contracting for hours straight. A contraction may last around 60 seconds, and then your body gives you a break. 

During my unmedicated labors, I really leaned into those spaces between contractions—completely relaxing, resetting, and only thinking about getting through the next minute when it came.

If you’re new here, hey! 👋 I’m Jess, i’ve had two beautiful unmedicated births, and I’m passionate about empowering women to educate themselves before birth. If this sounds like your thing, make sure to follow along. 🖤
